evidence: Varr. RR 3.1.1: rūstica et urbāna vīta (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of the city, as against rūsticus; at Rome, of Rome itself. Very often it means refined, polished, and witty: urbānitās is good manners and wit (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.240: senex quīdam oppidānus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of a country town rather than the capital, and so sometimes provincial, small-town; as a noun, oppidānī are the townspeople (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: annum ita dīvīsērunt, ut nōnīs modo diēbus urbānās rēs ūsurpārent, reliquīs septem ut rūra colerent
phrases.english: they divided the year so that they attended to town business only on every ninth day, and farmed the land on the other seven

phrases.latin: duae vītae hominum, rūstica et urbāna
phrases.english: the two ways men live, in the country and in the town

sources: Lewis & Short: urbanus · Lewis & Short: oppidanus
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-varro), checked against the editions named there. Varro’s Res rusticae III and Cicero as Lewis & Short quotes them.
